deleted.text: Skills for the full evidence-based preparation pipeline: research any topic with source verification, map its complete question space before you start, then write AI agent context that actually works — grounded instructions and disciplined reasoning instead of vibes.

[Research shows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988) LLM-generated context files do not generally improve agent task success while raising inference cost by 20–23% — and the repository overviews they typically contain are specifically unhelpful.
Rooted structurally refuses them: every rule traces to a peer-reviewed paper or an RFC.
Software-development and code-review skills apply the same discipline to everyday coding.
Every rule traces to a peer-reviewed paper, RFC/spec, or a hands-on test — not to "ask the model to write a skill."
Every rule, checklist item, and review criterion traces to one of:
**Academic research** — arxiv.org, peer-reviewed papers, Google Scholar, PubMed
**Technical standards** — RFCs, official specifications, language/framework documentation
**Human-tested** — a linked hands-on test (a commit or a gist) confirmed through practice
Three form a preparation pipeline — research → explore → write: gather verified sources, map every angle of a topic, then produce agent instructions grounded in evidence.

`/appraising-research` adds a critical-appraisal gate over a finished report — grading evidence quality, surfacing hidden assumptions, hunting competing hypotheses and blind spots, and mapping who benefits.
`/reading-companion` is an active-reading companion for a book you study yourself — grounded in learning-science research.
The last, `/handing-over-to-readers`, shapes what an agent hands to a human — a report, an explanation, a question, a client's question list — into a handover the reader checks against evidence.
Every new rule must cite a source — an arXiv ID, an RFC number, or a linked hands-on test.
PRs without citations are rejected by design, not by oversight.

candidates.sentence: Skills for the full evidence-based preparation pipeline: research any topic with source verification, map its complete question space before you start, then write AI agent context that actually works — grounded instructions and disciplined reasoning instead of vibes.

[Research shows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988) LLM-generated context files do not generally improve agent task success while raising inference cost by 20–23% — and the repository overviews they typically contain are specifically unhelpful.
Rooted admits rules by the scientific method instead: a claim rests on a test that could have refuted it, a norm is named as a norm and a decision as a decision.
**Tested, not asserted.**
A citation is the address of such a test, and where an idea came from carries no weight.
The method here is neither a sequence of steps nor a demand for a citation: it is a way of treating statements about how the world works.
A citation is the address of someone else's test and never the support itself; a test of our own, committed to the repository, counts the same.
An *opinion* names no outcome that would refute it and stays out of the rules.
every statement names its kind, and no kind passes for another
another person can repeat the test, or open its source and find the test there; an author's name supports nothing
No fitting
A claim of our own needs no citation.
Its hypothesis is committed first, the test runs with the technique and without it, and the result is committed after — a script reads that order from history.
The seven rules are a convention the repository adopts: the philosophy of science offers no single criterion of what is scientific, so the method takes what its main lines agree on.
A record is required on every rule line that is added or changed; the lines not yet touched carry their sources without a record.
A PR that offers a citation in place of a test is returned by design, not by oversight.

They are formulations of the method, read in the philosophy of science, and none of them is offered as a test of it; the line of each rule in [`method-provenance.md`](plugins/evidence-based-authoring/skills/testing-claims/maintenance/method-provenance.md) carries the passage it follows and how the text was seen.

[plato.stanford.edu/entries/scientific-method](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/scientific-method/) — No single universal method (§6.1); science differs from everyday knowledge by being more systematic (§7); the consequences of an error enter the choice between hypotheses (§4).

[plato.stanford.edu/entries/popper](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/popper/) — A scientific theory prohibits outcomes; only a risky prediction corroborates; a tested theory is corroborated and never verified (§3–5).

[Cambridge University Press, excerpt](https://assets.cambridge.org/97811076/64647/excerpt/9781107664647_excerpt.pdf) — The severity requirement: "One does not have evidence for a claim if nothing has been done to rule out ways the claim may be false."

[plato.stanford.edu/entries/scientific-objectivity](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/scientific-objectivity/) — Objectivity as testing by others (§5.2); values decide how much evidence suffices and are not themselves evidence (§3).
[plato.stanford.edu/entries/hume-moral](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/hume-moral/) — On the dominant reading, no evaluative conclusion follows from purely factual premises.

[plato.stanford.edu/entries/induction-problem](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/induction-problem/) — The step from observed cases to unobserved ones rests on a uniformity that reason does not establish (§1–2).

[plato.stanford.edu/entries/scientific-underdetermination](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/scientific-underdetermination/) — Duhem: an experiment tests a group of hypotheses and does not say which of them failed.

[plato.stanford.edu/entries/operationalism](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/operationalism/) — A concept tied to the operations that measure it (§2.1); no extension of a concept without operational grounds (§3.2).

[plato.stanford.edu/entries/physics-experiment](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/physics-experiment/), [plato.stanford.edu/entries/science-theory-observation](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/science-theory-observation/) — How an experimental result is validated, with no strategy guaranteeing it; observation depends on theory and still tests it.

[royalsociety.org/about-us/who-we-are/history](https://royalsociety.org/about-us/who-we-are/history/) — The motto *Nullius in verba*, "take nobody's word for it": statements are verified by an appeal to facts determined by experiment.

[iphlib.ru](https://iphlib.ru/library/collection/newphilenc/document/HASHde83409a66a4b8acacdcde) — A hypothesis is a scientific supposition whose truth value is undetermined; testability in principle is necessary and not sufficient.
7, as quoted at [wikiquote](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Richard_Feynman) — "It does not make any difference how smart you are, who made the guess, or what his name is.
